narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 55.5% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking in the third year of law school was the strongest reason the model leaned toward failure. Placing in the bottom decile (decile 1 out of 10) is substantially lower than the average of accepted students, who typically rank around the middle of their class. This low ranking strongly signaled higher risk of struggling on the bar.

Your LSAT score of 37 was the second most important factor and actually worked in your favor. It sits almost exactly at the average of students who were accepted, so it helped pull the prediction back toward passing. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.9 was the third most influential piece of information. While it also nudged the prediction slightly toward passing, the effect was much smaller than the negative impact of your third-year ranking.

Taken together, the model saw your recent law-school performance as the dominant signal that you were more likely than not to fail the bar, which led to the rejection.

What you should do next is focus on improving your class performance and consider retaking the bar-prep courses that target the specific areas where your third-year grades were weakest. Strengthening that record will have the biggest effect on future predictions.
